The PPE 3 build-out — the renewables roadmap to 2035
VII. PPE 3 BUILD-OUT

France's renewables build-out is governed by the third Programmation pluriannuelle de l'énergie (PPE 3) (Décret n° 2026-76, published 13 February 2026) which sets the country's energy strategy for 2026–2035: ~60% decarbonised energy by 2030, electricity consumption up ~40% by 2035, and a renewables programme delivered through CRE auctions. This section sets out the pathway from target to bankable contract, the capacity gap by technology, and the 2026–2027 tender calendar.

The PPE 3 pathway
VII-A. THE PPE 3 PATHWAY

Unlike a grid-connection queue, the French route to revenue is an auction pathway. PPE 3 fixes the capacity target and the volume to tender; the CRE designs the appel d'offres; and a project becomes bankable the moment it wins a complément de rémunération (CdR) — a ~20-year premium paid on top of the market price. RTE then funds and builds the offshore grid connection.

STEP 01
PPE 3 target
Decree n° 2026-76 sets the 2030 / 2035 capacity target per technology and the volumes the State will put to tender.
STEP 02
CRE tender designed
The Government refers the tender to the CRE, which issues its opinion (avis) on the cahier des charges (rules, volume, eligibility — incl. NZIA / resilience criteria).
STEP 03
Appel d'offres opens
A tendering period launches for a set volume (e.g. onshore 800 MW, solar 925 MWc, or the offshore AO9+AO10 ~10 GW round).
STEP 04
Competitive bid
Developers bid on price. Recent clearing: offshore fixed €66/MWh (AO8), solar ground-mount ~€74–79/MWh, onshore ~€80/MWh.
STEP 05
CdR award
Winner signs the complément de rémunération : revenue is de-risked over ~20 years. The bankability event.
STEP 06
Build & connect
Construction and grid connection (RTE for transmission / offshore; Enedis for distribution). Energise.
Investor Takeaway: the bankability event is the CdR award, not grid connection — diligence should centre on tender eligibility (environmental authorisation for onshore; NZIA / resilience sourcing for solar and offshore) and the CRE clearing price.

Investor Takeaway: the build-out gap concentrates in solar — best captured in load-rich southern zones (PACA, Occitanie) with the deepest irradiation, where co-located storage can capture the midday price spread. Onshore's gap is smaller and PPE 3 prioritises repowering, which reuses consented sites and existing connections. Agrivoltaics is explicitly prioritised in the plan.
When certainty arrives — the tender calendar
VII-C. THE AUCTION TIMELINE

PPE 3 was translated into a concrete tender calendar on 2 April 2026. Bankability arrives in three waves through 2026 and into early 2027: the near-term onshore and solar windows first, then a second onshore period and a technology-neutral solar tender, and finally the headline ~10 GW offshore round.

Investor Takeaway: the largest single pool of bankable capacity (high point of entry) is the offshore AO9+AO10 round (~10 GW, sub-€100/MWh target, RTE-funded connection) but with long build lead times. For near-term, lower-ticket deployment, the May / July 2026 onshore-repowering and ground-mount-solar windows are the fastest route to a CdR, especially in southern load zones.
The grid bottleneck — the primary barrier
VII. GRID CONNECTIONS

Everything in the technology section above runs into the same wall: a project cannot earn a penny until it is connected, and the queue for a firm connection is the binding constraint on the entire 2030 build-out. This section explains where the bottleneck is, how the reformed queue works, where capacity is scarce, and when certainty arrives.

Where the bottleneck is — the geography
VII-A. THE CONSTRAINT MAP

The GB grid is, at heart, a geography problem. Generation and demand sit at opposite ends of the network: Scotland hosts a large and growing share of the country's cheapest wind output, while demand is concentrated in the south, where data centre growth is adding further load.

The pinch point between them is the B6 boundary (the transmission interface between the SP Transmission network in southern Scotland and National Grid's network in northern England). B6's transfer capability is routinely exceeded by Scottish wind output, so the system operator pays northern generators to curtail while dispatching more expensive plant south of the boundary, a cost socialised across all consumers.

Constraint costs at this boundary are a structural feature of the market until new north–south capacity arrives, with the Eastern Green Link HVDC projects providing the first material relief from 2029.

The gated pathway to the network
VII-B. THE GATED PATHWAY

TMO4+ is a two-gate process. A project first earns a Gate 1 indicative offer, then must satisfy both a Readiness test and a Strategic Alignment test to reach Gate 2 — a firm offer carrying a confirmed date, connection point and queue position. Gate 2 projects are then split into Phase 1 (2030 delivery) and Phase 2 (2035). This module covers transmission and large embedded connections only.

STEP 01
Application
Project applies in a connections window. ~3,000 applications were assessed in the queue-reordering exercise (G2tWQ).
STEP 02
Gate 1
Indicative offer + queue position based on a coordinated network design. No confirmed connection date.
STEP 03
Gate 2 criteria
Must pass both: Readiness (land + planning) and Strategic Alignment (needed for the plan).
STEP 04
Gate 2 offer
Firm offer: confirmed date, connection point and queue position. The bankability event.
STEP 05
Milestones
Queue Management Milestones. M1 = initiate statutory consents & submit planning. Miss them and you can be removed.
STEP 06
Energise
Build and connect. Phase 1 targets 2030 delivery; Phase 2 targets 2035.
Pipeline by technology — where the scarcity is
VII-C. THE CAPACITY SIGNAL

The clearest deal-flow signal in the reform. Each bar is the prioritised Gate 2 pipeline (Phase 1 + Phase 2); the dot marks the Gate 1 overhang, i.e. capacity that applied but was not prioritised. Where the dot sits far beyond the bar, the market is crowded with projects seeking capital and investors can be selective on terms (battery). Where the dot is tiny, nearly every project that wanted a connection got one, so opportunities are fewer and holders of a Gate 2 position carry a premium (offshore wind, interconnectors).

Where the bottleneck is — the geography
VII. THE NORTH–SOUTH CONSTRAINT

Germany's grid is a geography problem. Cheap wind generation concentrates in the north and east; demand sits in the south and west: Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg and the Ruhr. The transmission network between them cannot yet carry the surplus, so northern wind is curtailed and southern conventional (mainly coal) plant is ramped up. The cost (€3.07 bn in 2025) is socialised through network tariffs under a single national price, and closes only as the four HVDC corridors energise from 2027 to 2030. Batteries and other flexibility technologies sited at or behind the congestion charge cheap (curtailed/negative-priced) northern power and discharge into the expensive southern peak, monetising spreads that exist because the HVDC corridors are not yet in service. The window is structural but time-bound: the alpha is largest now and compresses as SuedLink/SuedOstLink energise from 2027–2030, so secured-grid-connection sites in or near the bottleneck are the asset to own.
